items.title: Asiedu Nketia urges police to act against vote-buying in party elections
items.description: The National Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Johnson Asiedu Nketia, has urged the police and other security agencies to investigate and take appropriate action against anyone found engaging in criminal conduct during internal political party elections. He said allegations of vote-buying should not be treated merely as disciplinary matters for political parties, insisting that state institutions had a responsibility to enforce the country’s laws regardless of the political affiliation of those involved. Speaking in an interview with JoyNews on Friday, November 13, Mr Asiedu Nketia said while it was not wrong for individuals to support party members, the practice became unacceptable when gifts and financial inducements were used to influence voting and secure political positions. “It is not a bad thing if anybody wants to give party people something. But if it happens in a way around elections to suggest that we are just buying positions, then it is not acceptable at all in a democracy,” he said. He called on the security agencies not to hesitate to act whenever they encountered conduct that breached criminal laws, arguing that party regulations alone were inadequate to deal with such offences. “Once you are citizens and we are all subject to the laws of this country, when you want to subordinate the national laws to party laws, that’s not correct. Then you are part of the problem,” he said. Mr Asiedu Nketia said political parties had their own responsibility to caution members and enforce internal rules, but that responsibility should not prevent state institutions from intervening where criminal conduct was suspected. “The security services should be bold to proceed with whatever measures they want to do the same way as they deal with crime anywhere else,” he added. He further argued that law enforcement agencies should not wait for the leadership of the NDC or the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) to take disciplinary action before responding to suspected criminal offences. “If there is criminality, state institutions should not sit there and say that this is an NPP matter. It is an NDC matter. So you are waiting for NDC chairman to act this way. I’m waiting for NPP chairman to act this way,” he said. Debate over vote-buying in party primaries The comments come amid persistent concerns about the use of money and material inducements to influence delegates during internal party elections. The issue attracted renewed public attention following allegations of inducements during the NDC parliamentary primary in Ayawaso East in February 2026. The Office of the Special Prosecutor opened an investigation into claims that television sets had been distributed to delegates. The allegations generated calls for stronger measures to protect the credibility of party elections. The controversy also exposed a gap in Ghana’s electoral laws. While Section 33 of the Representation of the People Law, 1992 (PNDCL 284) criminalises bribery intended to influence voters in public elections, existing legislation does not expressly extend the same electoral offences to internal party contests. In March 2026, Speaker of Parliament Alban Bagbin announced that a Private Members’ Bill seeking to address misconduct during party primaries and by-elections was before Parliament. The proposed reforms were intended to extend criminal sanctions to vote-buying and other forms of electoral malpractice in internal party elections. Mr Asiedu Nketia’s latest comments therefore add to the debate over how political parties and state institutions should respond to alleged inducements in internal contests. He said he was pleased that the party’s incoming leadership shared his concern about the monetisation of internal elections, expressing confidence that the fight against the practice would continue beyond his tenure as chairman. He maintained that protecting the integrity of party elections was a responsibility that extended beyond party executives to the country’s law enforcement institutions.

items.title: Egemen Mustafa Şener on the three words he learned in a Black Sea village that still run his business
items.description: Çifteköprü is a small village in the Borçka district of Artvin, in Türkiye’s Eastern Black Sea region. It is the kind of place where the weather decides more of the week than any calendar does, where a neighbour’s word carries the same weight as a document, and where the ground gives back exactly what the work put in. It is also where Egemen Mustafa Şener learned, before he ever ran a construction site in Istanbul or a shipyard project in Montevideo, the three practices that still organise his business today. The three words, as the company itself frames them, are labor, promises, and land. From a Black Sea farm to an Istanbul construction site Şener was born in Çifteköprü in May 1968. His father worked the land, his mother came from a well-established Laz family, and the household ran on a set of unspoken rules that any rural community would recognise. Work was visible or it hadn’t happened. A spoken commitment was binding. The land did not reward shortcuts. When he moved to Istanbul after high school, into business school and then into agricultural trading in the late 1980s, those rules didn’t get left behind. By the early 1990s, when he had shifted into residential and commercial construction and was managing his first sites in the city, the same three practices were doing the actual work of running the business. The language of the construction industry was new, but the habits underneath it were the same ones he had grown up with. Egemen Mustafa Şener on labor, in a sector where everything has to be seen The first of the three is labor, and in construction it is not a metaphor. Every person on a site contributes something that is either visible in the finished work or hidden inside it. A good site manager is one who can see the work that is supposed to be hidden as clearly as the work on the surface. Visible labor is also what makes delivery possible. A project is a stack of promises about what will happen on which date, and every one of those promises rests on someone actually doing the work. When labor becomes abstract, delivery slips. In three decades of residential, commercial, industrial and infrastructure projects, this has not changed. The promise that does the work before the contract does The second word is promises. In most business settings, promises are secondary to contracts. In the one Egemen Mustafa Şener grew up in, they were the contract. A spoken commitment was held because the alternative, in a village the size of Çifteköprü, was impossible to live with. Transplanted into construction, that habit becomes a working style. A contract will specify the delivery date and the quality standard. But between any two reasonable parties, the real agreement is the one that was given before the paperwork caught up, and the business that honours that version tends to finish projects on terms that match what was actually said. In his international expansion into Ukraine, Eastern Europe, and the Montevideo-to-Recife shipyard corridor in South America, the legal frameworks have changed with every border. The practice of honouring the spoken commitment has not. Land, and the kind of value that takes root The third word is land. For a farming family on the Eastern Black Sea, land was both livelihood and measure. You couldn’t fake it, you couldn’t speculate your way through it, and what you put in over years was what you got back. In construction, infrastructure, port and shipyard investment, this habit shows up as a preference for assets that keep standing when the market cycle ends. Buildings that are still useful decades after handover. Infrastructure that keeps cities working. Ports that serve real trade. The three-word discipline keeps selecting for these over faster-return options. items.title: Police begin rolling out TraffiTech-GH speed camera warning signs after Mahama directive
items.description: The Ghana Police Service and road safety agencies have commenced processes for the installation of large advance warning signboards across key road corridors to alert motorists to the presence of automated TraffiTech-GH speed cameras. The move follows a direct call by President John Dramani Mahama for administrative transparency in the deployment of the automated traffic enforcement system, insisting that drivers must be given clear prior notice of camera locations. Photographs from the exercise show police personnel and technical crews preparing and mounting large blue-and-yellow reflective gantries equipped with heavy lifting machinery. In one of the photos, ACP Alexander Kwaku Obeng, Director of Education, Research and Training at the MTTD, was captured by some of the signs bearing a 50 m speed limit sign. Some of the newly introduced billboards prominently feature a camera icon alongside a red-ringed “80” km/h speed limit sign. Bold inscriptions on the panels read: “24-hrs speed camera monitoring” and “Speed kills, kill it now” . Fulfilling the transparency mandate The signage rollout directly addresses public concerns raised following the launch of the TraffiTech-GH initiative on November 1, 2026. Several commercial transport operators and private motorists had criticized the initial phase of the system, arguing that enforcing automated fines without visible warning signs amounted to entrapment. Speaking on the sidelines of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda earlier this month, President Mahama backed the technology as vital to reducing pedestrian fatalities while directing the police and implementing partners to erect visible advance notices. “All I will urge is that the police and those implementing TraffiTech should put signs showing where the cameras are, because that is one of the things you need to do if you are introducing this kind of innovation,” President Mahama stated. “You need to put signposts warning motorists that there is a speed camera ahead. I think that transparency is important.” How the TraffiTech-GH system operates Operated under the Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) of the Ghana Police Service, TraffiTech-GH uses fixed, mobile, and radar camera sensors to capture speeding violations in real time. Once a vehicle exceeds the posted speed limit, the system automatically generates an Electronic Notice of Violation (ENV) and dispatches an SMS alert containing details of the infraction and statutory fine to the registered owner’s mobile phone. Road safety officials have indicated that the ongoing installation of warning signs will be extended across major highways and urban arteries nationwide as authorities prepare to activate additional enforcement modules covering red-light jumping and illegal parking.

items.title: Lumumba identifies what’s fueling xenophobia
items.description: •Says Africa cannot fight poverty by turning against fellow Africans Professor Patrick Loch Otieno (PLO) Lumumba has warned that Africa’s failure to create sufficient economic opportunities is fuelling xenophobia. He urged governments to address unemployment, poverty and weak industrial development rather than blame migrants for the continent’s challenges. Lumumba, a renowned Kenyan legal scholar and public speaker, said xenophobia often thrived in societies experiencing economic hardship, where unemployment, inequality and pressure on public services encouraged citizens to regard foreigners as competitors. He spoke as the keynote speaker at the Bridge Club’s grand end-of-year event in Lagos on Thursday. In his address, titled Africa Must Not Become Foreign to Itself: Xenophobia, Pan-Africanism and the Future of African Belonging, Lumumba argued that migrants were frequently made scapegoats for economic problems arising from poor governance and weak institutions. He said: “The foreign trader, worker or entrepreneur can be arrested. The failure to create productive employment over several decades cannot be arrested at a roadblock.” According to him, African governments must look beyond the presence of migrants and examine the structural weaknesses responsible for unemployment, poverty and economic competition. He said the inability of many African countries to industrialise and create productive jobs had forced millions of young people into informal economic activities, where competition for limited opportunities could generate resentment. Lumumba observed that Africa’s economic dependence on exporting raw materials while importing finished products had contributed to the loss of employment opportunities to other economies. “We export crude oil and import refined petroleum. We export cocoa and import chocolate. We export minerals and import the machines, batteries and technologies manufactured from them,” he said. He added that the continent was effectively creating employment opportunities elsewhere while its young population continued to struggle for limited opportunities at home. The legal scholar said the appropriate response to the exploitation of migrant workers was to enforce labour laws against employers rather than encourage hostility towards foreigners. According to him, employers who engage undocumented migrants and pay them below lawful wages create resentment among local workers while benefiting from the division. “The appropriate response is not violence against the migrant. It is enforcement of labour law against the employer,” he said. Lumumba also highlighted the contradiction in Africans celebrating the achievements of their compatriots abroad while treating migrants from other African countries with hostility. He noted that Nigerians seeking opportunities in London, Kenyans travelling to Dubai, Ghanaians moving to Canada and Zimbabweans relocating to South Africa were motivated by the same desire to improve their living conditions. “We therefore understand perfectly well why human beings migrate when opportunity is scarce. We simply become less understanding when the migrant arrives at our own door,” he said. He stressed that African governments must recognise their responsibility to create jobs, protect wages, improve public services and enforce immigration laws without subjecting foreigners to humiliation or collective punishment. Lumumba maintained that the fight against xenophobia was inseparable from the struggle for economic development, insisting that African economies must become sufficiently productive to accommodate their growing populations. “The real enemy is therefore not the African who crosses the border in search of opportunity. The greater enemy is an economic order that creates too little opportunity and then invites Africans to quarrel over the little that exists,” he said. He urged African leaders to prioritise industrialisation, agricultural transformation, infrastructure development, education and technology as sustainable measures for tackling economic hardship and reducing hostility towards migrants. Lumumba said Pan-Africanism must move beyond declarations of solidarity to practical economic cooperation capable of making the prosperity of one African country beneficial to others. Earlier, the President of The Bridge Club, Abdulhakeem Mustapha (SAN), said the continued discrimination against Africans in other African countries represented a fundamental contradiction of the ideals of continental unity. He said Pan-Africanism must be reflected in everyday conduct, institutional practices and the way African countries treat citizens of other African nations. “How can we preach Pan-Africanism while tolerating attitudes and practices that diminish the humanity and dignity of fellow Africans?” he asked. items.title: 2027: Violence threatens turnout as party supporters come under attacks
items.description: •60 to 70 per cent of voters afraid of voting – security analyst •INEC warns of N10m fine, jail term for inflammatory campaigns •Attacks on rallies, convoys heighten fears By Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA: Between 60 to 70 per cent of Nigerian voters are afraid that political violence will stop them from voting in 2027, a security expert, Mr Onyekachi Adekoya, has said, as voter apathy continues to rise. Adekoya spoke on Friday morning on The Morning Brief, a programme on Channels Television. He cited a calculation by Yiaga Africa. “If you look at Yiaga Africa’s calculation, 60 to 70% of voters are worried that political violence will not allow them come out on the day,” he said. He said that fear works against turnout. “Once the violence and the rhetoric of it goes up, people are less likely to come out to vote, and perhaps that is, some would argue, part of the strategy at play by some parties,” he said. There have been recent incidents, including attacks on party convoys and on an assembly in some states including Delta, Cross River, Lagos, Edo and Gombe states. In Delta State, a man was apprehended and not handed over to the police. He was then reportedly killed. Adekoya said violence was already rising and would get worse. “It is already ticking over 70 incidents captured so far,” he said. “This is not the peak of it because the campaign season has just started.” He said the stakes went beyond 2027, with politicians positioning for 2031 and 2039. “We expect that this political season will be a bit more violent and true to type,” he said. He said pressure on local politicians would raise tensions. “Politicians at the local level are under significant pressure to deliver on their areas and that would most likely raise tensions. What it will look like is that politicians use violence to destabilize the opponents in opponents’ area of strength so that they can lose votes.” Adekoya said his firm’s report classed 14 states as toss-up states, which would be “keenly contested”. He named the North Central, North East and North West, and parts of the South East, as areas of concern. “Nobody should die because somebody is trying to be president,” he said. On what security agencies could do, Adekoya said the shortfall lay in resources. “If at all there is a failure in security it is because of lack of capacity, poor logistics planning and the fact that we have a hydraheaded security problem which cannot be resolved,” he said. He said enforcement could not be left to the agencies alone. “There is a command structure where also politics get in the way of enforcement. It should not be a job only for the police, it should be a collective responsibility,” he said. The concerns followed a run of threats by office holders in several states in recent weeks, which has drawn condemnation from civil society groups, rights organisations and opposition politicians. In Osun State, Senator Francis Adenigba Fadahunsi (Osun East) was questioned by the Nigeria Police Force over a viral video. He was heard telling supporters in Ilesa: “Until the day of election, when you see any Accord party member here in Ilesa, kill them.” Governor Ademola Adeleke rejected the senator’s clarification, called the remarks a national security threat and demanded his arrest. In the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), the Chairman of Kuje Area Council, Mr Samuel Danjuma Shekwolo, warned residents who do not support his party to relocate ahead of 2027. Amnesty International Nigeria condemned the remarks as a “call to violence.” In Borno State, the Commissioner for Youth and Sports Development, Mr Sainna Buba, said those who refuse to support the ruling party in 2027 “will be flogged.” He also warned that anyone who crossed the party would have a finger broken. In Kebbi State, the Chairman of Gwandu Local Government Area, Alhaji Atiku Ahmad Mandiya, told supporters that anyone who spoke against Governor Nasir Idris “should be dealt with.” The International Republican Institute (IRI) said civil society monitors recorded more than 81 election-related violent incidents in Osun State alone in the year before the August governorship poll. A Pre-Election Security Risk Assessment by the Kimpact Development Initiative (KDI) documented 73 election-related violent incidents, with 29 deaths, ahead of local polls in the state. Against this backdrop, the Independent National Electoral Commission INEC has warned that politicians and parties who use abusive, intemperate or inflammatory language risk fines and imprisonment under the Electoral Act 2026. INEC’s Chief Press Secretary/Media Adviser to the Chairman, Mr Adedayo Oketola, said campaign rhetoric becomes punishable once it moves beyond policy critique. “Under the Nigerian legal framework, rhetoric becomes punishable intimidation when it incites ethnic, religious, or regional hostility through abusive, base, or slanderous language explicitly designed to provoke violent emotions or target specific groups,” Oketola said, citing Section 96 of the Act. Quoting the law and attendant penalties, he said: “A political campaign or slogan shall not be tainted with abusive language directly or indirectly likely to injure religious, ethnic, tribal or sectional feelings. Any candidate who commits these offences is liable upon conviction to a maximum fine of ₦5,000,000 or imprisonment for a term of 12 months. “A non-compliant political party is liable to a fine of ₦10,000,000 in the first instance, and ₦2,000,000 for each subsequent offence.” Oketola said INEC is an election management body, not a security agency. “The Commission can issue formal queries and sanction non-compliant parties within its administrative limits,” he said. He said the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies have a duty to prevent a breakdown of law and order, while the media and traditional and religious leaders should discourage inflammatory language. “Political campaigns should be platforms of competing ideas, not theatres of war,” Oketola said. items.title: Sacking of Atiku: What Justice Lifu based his judgement on
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA – The leadership crisis rocking the African Democratic Congress (ADC) took a decisive turn when Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, invalidated the emergence of Senator David Mark and other executives who assumed control of the party in July 2025. But the judgment of November 5, 2026, was not simply about competing claims to party leadership. It hinged on a fundamental legal question: could the party’s National Executive Committee (NEC) use its constitutional powers to replace an existing elected leadership structure without complying with the democratic procedures prescribed by law? In the Certified True Copy (CTC) of the judgment obtained by Saturday Vanguard, Justice Lifu said he identified critical weaknesses in the defendants’ case, including the disputed resignation letter on which they relied, the limits of NEC’s administrative powers and the absence of satisfactory evidence that the new executives emerged through a democratic election. The resignation letter One of the Mark-led camp’s principal arguments was that Nafiu Bala Gombe had voluntarily resigned as Deputy National Chairman on May 17, 2025, before the NEC meeting that produced the new leadership. The letter, tendered as Exhibit ADC 1, was intended to establish that Gombe had relinquished his position and consequently lacked the legal standing to challenge the subsequent leadership transition. Justice Lifu, however, was unconvinced Rather than accept the document simply because it was certified, the judge examined its signature against Gombe’s signatures on other documents executed before a Commissioner for Oaths. He explained that certification established the status of a document as a true copy but did not, in itself, establish the authenticity of a disputed signature. After comparing the documents, he said that he found material differences in their structure, style, formation and general manner of execution. “The signatures do not appear to be one and the same,” Justice Lifu observed. He consequently described the purported resignation letter as fictitious or fabricated and rejected it as reliable evidence that Gombe had voluntarily vacated his office. The finding removed a central pillar of the defendants’ argument that Gombe had ceased to be an officer of the party before the July 2025 transition. Importantly, this was a finding made in determining the civil dispute, not a criminal conviction for forgery. NEC’s powers could not override the law The second major issue concerned the extent of NEC’s authority under Article 19(14) of the ADC constitution. The defendants maintained that the provision empowered NEC to dissolve the existing National Working Committee (NWC), make administrative arrangements and install the new executives. Justice Lifu acknowledged that political parties enjoy autonomy in managing their internal affairs However, he held that such autonomy must operate within the limits of the Constitution and applicable electoral legislation. He relied on Section 223(1)(a) of the 1999 Constitution, which requires political parties to provide for periodic democratic elections of their principal officers and executive committees. He also considered Sections 82(1) and 82(3) of the Electoral Act 2022, alongside the relevant provisions of the Regulations and Guidelines for Political Parties, 2022. His reasoning was that although NEC could exercise administrative powers under the party constitution, those powers could not be interpreted to dispense with mandatory democratic procedures. In effect, the authority to administer a political party was not an unrestricted licence to appoint its national executives in place of a legally required election. Emergence if new Excos The decisive weakness in the defendants’ case, according to the judge, was the absence of satisfactory evidence that the new executives emerged through a democratic electoral process. The defendants relied on documents showing that INEC had received notice of the NEC meeting, monitored its proceedings and subsequently recognised the resulting leadership. But Justice Lifu drew a clear distinction between notifying INEC and conducting a democratic election. He held that the Commission’s monitoring of the meeting did not establish that party members or duly elected delegates were given the opportunity to participate and vote for candidates of their choice. The judge explained that notice to INEC and compliance with democratic election requirements were separate legal obligations. Consequently, neither the Commission’s attendance nor its subsequent recognition could validate a process that had not been shown to comply with the law. The court therefore found no satisfactory evidence that the emergence of Mark and the other executives was preceded by, or resulted from, a democratic election as required by Section 82(3) of the Electoral Act. This was central to the outcome: the defendants could not establish the legality of their emergence merely by demonstrating that INEC had been notified of, and monitored, the NEC meeting. Internal-party-affairs argument The defendants also challenged the court’s jurisdiction, arguing that the dispute concerned the internal affairs of a political party and was therefore unsuitable for judicial intervention. Justice Lifu rejected that position Relying on the Supreme Court’s decision in Peoples Democratic Party v. Sule Lamido & Ors., he reasoned that although courts should ordinarily avoid interfering in internal political preferences, they cannot stand aside when a party’s actions are alleged to violate express constitutional or statutory provisions. He also rejected the argument that Gombe had to exhaust the party’s internal dispute-resolution mechanisms before approaching the court. The judge held that the objection was insufficient in the circumstances because the dispute raised questions of compliance with constitutional and statutory obligations. The court was therefore entitled to determine whether the leadership transition complied with the law. What the judge finally ordered Having resolved the substantive issues in Gombe’s favour, Justice Lifu invalidated the emergence of Mark and the other disputed executives, nullified the resolutions of the ADC’s 99th NEC meeting of July 29, 2025, and restrained the affected executives from presenting themselves as officers of the party. He also declared Gombe the only elected NWC member whose four-year tenure remained in force and who was legally entitled to supervise the party’s affairs. However, the judge expressly distinguished this entitlement from automatic succession to the office of National Chairman. That distinction is important. The judgment did not automatically install Gombe as National Chairman; rather, it affirmed his continuing status as the elected NWC member whose tenure remained valid and recognised his legal entitlement to supervise the party’s affairs. Ultimately, Gombe succeeded because the court found that his purported resignation had not been established, NEC’s administrative powers could not override constitutional and statutory requirements, and the Mark-led executives had failed to demonstrate that their emergence followed the legally prescribed democratic process. The central message of Justice Lifu’s decision was that a political party cannot use its internal constitution to circumvent the Constitution of the country. items.title: ‘I may lose my mind’: Frustrated travelers stuck in US flight havoc
items.description: Confusion reigned at airports across the United States on Friday, as a rare grounding of all US flights stranded hundreds of thousands of frustrated travellers with no end to the delays in sight. In New York’s busy LaGuardia airport, Janice Llewellyn was on the verge of tears: the chaos could mean she will miss her daughter’s wedding in Toronto. The 61-year-old Llewellyn was desperate to find an alternative route, telling AFP : “I may lose my mind.” “My husband flew all the way from England to get to the wedding,” she said. “Oh gosh! I wish they had another flight, I wish I could get another flight, like, now.” Planes wait at the terminal of LaGuardia Airport, New York on November 13, 2026. US aviation regulators issued an extremely rare ground stop of all flights across the country November 13 after a major communications outage which the Department of Homeland Security said did not appear to be the result of any “nefarious attack.” — AFP At the airport in Las Vegas, some fliers were told their journeys were delayed due to wind. One airline staffer said the ground stop would last eight hours. Another said 24 hours. Government officials have said the grounding was due to a major communications outage and not due to any “nefarious attack.” But that didn’t help travellers understand what comes next. People wait to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. The Federal Aviation Administration on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” — AFP The shambolic lack of information led many passengers to form long lines at rental car counters in a mad dash for travel alternatives. Joseph Anderson said he was trying to get back to Oakland from Vegas and was considering driving — but said, “if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too.” And the 72-year-old retired Air Force veteran said his already-checked luggage was captive, meaning “we’re kind of stuck.” “I would hope the communication can be better from the FAA,” he said. People sit on the floor as they wait to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. The Federal Aviation Administration on Friday ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” — AFP Friday the 13th The ground stop comes less than two weeks before the Thanksgiving holiday, the busiest travel moment of the year in the United States. And it falls ahead of a particularly busy weekend for professional and college sports — teams and their fans are also stuck. Back in New York, Tiara Johnson had been heading to Orlando for a weekend concert, and any hope that she would make it was growing dim. “You think you’re gonna be there in three hours, but your whole evening is kind of done!” the 50-year-old told AFP . “But hey, they say it’s Friday the 13th!” Harried passengers stared at their phones, calm but annoyed, wandering the airport terminal without clear direction. Hagit Levy Shalev, 54, was zen. She booked a new flight for Saturday morning, meaning her work trip would last a little longer. “I’ll get there,” she laughed. “One more extra day away from the kids!”

items.title: Asiedu Nketia satisfied with NDC legacy as he prepares to exit chairmanship
items.description: The National Chairman of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Johnson Asiedu Nketia, says he is leaving the party in a stronger position than he found it when he assumed office in December 2022. He said the retention of key members of the party’s national leadership was an indication that the team had delivered on its mandate, expressing satisfaction with the work done during his tenure. Speaking in an interview with JoyNews on Friday, November 13, Mr Asiedu Nketia said he was particularly pleased that the party had maintained some experienced hands in key positions. “I’m happy that even at the national level, this is about the first time that we are retaining key people in their positions. It is a recognition that this team has done what is expected of us,” he said. Reflecting on his election as chairman at the party’s 2022 National Delegates Congress at the Accra Sports Stadium, he recalled the commitment he made to lead the NDC through what he described as a difficult political period. He said his team had faced a government that, in his assessment, was determined to hold on to power and had the financial and state security resources to do so. “When we were elected at the sports stadium, I gave a commitment on behalf of my team that we are in to fight a very difficult battle because we had a government that was unyielding and was prepared to use money, prepared to use the coercive forces of state, and so on,” he said. Mr Asiedu Nketia said the team remained resolute despite the challenges, insisting that determination among party members was more powerful than the resources available to those in government. “I did say that the most powerful army in the world cannot defeat people who are determined to change their circumstances for the better,” he said. He added that he had confidence in the people he worked with and was satisfied that their efforts had helped the party return to government. A handover he says he is proud of The outgoing chairman said his greatest satisfaction was not simply the political gains made under his leadership but the state of the party’s organisation at the end of his tenure. He said he had sought to leave the party’s headquarters and structures in better condition than he inherited them. “My satisfaction is that I’m leaving the NDC headquarters better than how I came to meet it. And that is what gives me my satisfaction,” he said. Mr Asiedu Nketia was elected NDC National Chairman in December 2022, defeating incumbent Samuel Ofosu Ampofo at the party’s 10th National Delegates Congress. Before then, he had served as the party’s General Secretary for 17 years. He has decided not to seek another term as chairman, bringing his current leadership tenure to an end as the party prepares to elect new national executives at its December 19, 2026, delegates congress. The party’s ongoing executive election process has already produced some uncontested positions. Incumbent General Secretary Fifi Fiavi Kwetey, National Organiser Joseph Yammin and Communications Officer Godwin Ako Gunn are among those who have no opponents after vetting. The congress will determine the next team to lead the NDC as it prepares for the next phase of its political activities.

items.title: Pourquoi il faut prêter attention à la courbe de popularité de Poutine
items.description: Selon les derniers sondages réalisés par le Levada Center, la principale ONG indépendante qui continue de travailler sur l’opinion publique russe, la popularité de Vladimir Poutine a chuté de 8 points en un an. Elle se situait en octobre à 77 %, soit en légère hausse (+3 points) par rapport au mois de juin (74 %) Рейтинги октября 2026 года : настроения, оценки положения дел в стране, одобрение органов власти, рейтинги политиков и партий , Levada Center, 30 octobre 2026.'> 1 . Poutine, qui exerce le pouvoir en Russie depuis plus de 25 ans, à la tête du gouvernement et à la présidence, a connu plusieurs chutes de sa popularité. En 2005 notamment, la décision de monétiser les avantages sociaux, c'est-à-dire de remplacer les avantages en nature dont bénéficiaient les retraités, comme les transports gratuits ou les médicaments, par des compensations financières jugées insuffisantes, avait conduit des dizaines de milliers de personnes à descendre dans les rues. Dans les semaines qui ont suivi le début du mouvement, le gouvernement est revenu partiellement sur ce changement, puis Poutine a lancé, en septembre, de vastes programmes de dépenses publiques dans les domaines de la santé, du logement, de l’éducation et de l’agriculture. Après cet épisode de 2005, se sont ensuivies deux baisses structurelles de la cote de Poutine dans les sondages : de 2011 à 2013, puis de 2018 à 2021. En avril 2020, durant la pandémie de coronavirus, la popularité de Poutine était passée sous la barre des 60 % pour la première fois depuis septembre 1999 dans les séries du Levada Center. Dans les deux cas, des opérations militaires majeures lui ont offert un bond quasi instantané dans les enquêtes d’opinion. Entre novembre 2013 et novembre 2014, soit huit mois après l’annexion de la Crimée, la popularité du président russe a bondi de 24 points, passant de 61 % à 85 % de taux d’approbation, dont 11 points dans le seul mois de l’annexion. Le lancement de l’invasion à grande échelle de l’Ukraine, en février 2022, a quant à lui donné lieu à une hausse de 22 points en l’espace d’un an, entre août 2021 et août 2022, dont 12 points entre février et mars 2022. Les politistes parlent d’effet de ralliement autour du drapeau. Les guerres, comme les attaques terroristes d’ampleur ou les catastrophes, ont tendance à changer l’orientation émotionnelle de la population, au profit des dirigeants en place : la fierté et l’espoir prennent le pas sur la colère et l’inquiétude, et l’action du pouvoir est jugée plus favorablement, y compris dans des domaines sans rapport avec la crise. En extrapolant à partir des chiffres du Levada Center, Poutine pourrait se retrouver au point où il en était avant 2014 et avant 2022 entre l’été 2027 et le milieu de 2028. Plusieurs témoignages indiquent que Poutine se préoccupe des résultats de ces enquêtes d’opinion. Son entourage est toutefois moins disposé qu’auparavant à lui montrer des sondages défavorables : en 2022, le sociologue Sergueï Khaïkine a voulu faire remonter à Poutine des données montrant l’opposition à la guerre parmi la jeunesse. Des responsables du Kremlin lui auraient alors répondu : « Il ne faut pas contrarier Vladimir Vladimirovitch » Ненатуральные числа. Часть вторая », Проект , 7 juillet 2022.'> 2 . L’article Pourquoi il faut prêter attention à la courbe de popularité de Poutine est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: NPA reduces price floor for petrol to GH¢13.69, diesel to GH¢16.73
items.description: The price of petrol per litre is expected to fall further from November 16, 2026, by some significant margin, while that of diesel would also go down marginally. This is coming after the National Petroleum Authority, together with industry players, reviewed the price floor for petrol from GH¢15.39 per litre to GH¢13.69 for the November 16 to 30, 2026, pricing window. This actually represents an almost 13% decline from the old price quotes that the NPA put out some two weeks ago. On the other hand, diesel will go down to GH¢16.73 per litre from the previous price of GH¢17.41. LPG will also witness a significant increase, from GH¢13.73 per kilogramme to GH¢15.93. According to the NPA, this excludes premiums charged by International Oil Trading Companies, operating margins of Bulk Import, Distribution and Export Companies, and margins charged by Oil Marketing Companies and LPG Marketing Companies. The respective companies will determine those charges independently under the prescribed Petroleum Products Pricing Formula. Implications The adjustments could produce mixed price movements at the pumps during the next pricing window. Lower price floors could give marketers room to reduce petrol and LPG prices. However, final adjustments will depend on the premiums and margins individual companies apply. However, based on past developments, there are strong indications that the price of petrol could go down further, while that of diesel and LPG may go up. Some of the oil marketing firms have already indicated that they will drop the price of petrol and even that of diesel. The major oil marketing firm, Star Oil, for instance, had reduced prices three times over the past week and is now selling a litre of petrol at GH¢15.55 and diesel going for GH¢18.37. Another player in the industry, Allied Oil, has also reviewed prices at the pumps, selling a litre of petrol at GH¢15.50 and diesel at GH¢18.20. JP has also reduced its petrol price from GH¢16.43 quoted on October 16 to GH¢15.95. The price of diesel has also been reduced to GH¢18.35 from GH¢18.97. Under the current regulations governing the pricing of petroleum products, prices are supposed to be reviewed on the 1st and 16th of each month. However, the NPA has maintained that oil marketing companies can proceed with price reviews at the pumps, provided the adjustments are in line with the guidelines sanctioned by the market regulator. The Ghana cedi has been fairly stable, while the International Energy Agency has projected that global oil markets will swing to supply surplus for the first time since the start of the Iran War as Persian Gulf exports recover. Background The Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies (COMAC) attributed the mixed reviews in prices of petroleum products to the cedi’s appreciation and the reduced prices of finished petroleum products and crude oil on the international market.

items.title: US flights resume after FAA lifts hours-long nationwide ground stop
items.description: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that halted departing flights across the United States for more than four hours after a “communication issue” affected air traffic control centres. The FAA announced at 8:15pm Eastern time on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday) that it had lifted the order, after it issued the ground stop hours earlier at 3:54pm (20:54 GMT). Airlines face delays and cancellations as they get aircraft and crews back into position. The FAA said in a post on X in the afternoon that there had been a “temporary telecommunications outage” and that, as a precaution, all flights were being halted. International flights would be handled case by case, it added. More than 10,000 flights were delayed and over 4,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware, CBS News reported.Some 4,042 flights were in the air, heading to US airports, when the ground stop was ordered, according to the tracking site Flightradar24. The communication issue affected all 22 air route traffic control centres, which guide aircraft. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication that the ground stop was triggered by a threat to the US. “Everybody’s safe. The flights are accounted for,” he said. “This is not another 9/11.” Trump’s silence questioned US President Donald Trump has not addressed the situation and has remained absent from the public scene since the FAA announced the ground stop. Trump has been “fully engaged” in responding to the nationwide flight shutdown, Mullin said after a reporter asked during a White House news conference why the president had not spoken publicly about the disruption. “I don’t run the president’s comms,” Mullin replied, saying Trump had been in regular contact with senior officials since the crisis began. Mullin also said the president had spoken with officials multiple times and had been briefed on developments throughout the disruption. The homeland security secretary also defended Trump, saying the president had been pushing for an overhaul of the country’s ageing air traffic control infrastructure. Passengers wait as flights are delayed at Seattle-Tacoma international airport in Seattle, Washington, on November 13, 2026 [Lindsey Wasson/AP] Asked whether a planned rollout of a new AI tool meant to help air traffic controllers could be to blame, Mullin said officials have not ruled it out. “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We are going through that process,” he said. The FBI does not believe a cyberattack or criminal activity caused the failure, Bloomberg reported, citing an official familiar with the matter. The cited official said investigators were examining whether a software update could have caused the outage, though the cause had not been determined. Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth has called for a “thorough and complete investigation” of the reported FAA communication issues. “The safety of our skies is built on redundancies. Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation,” Duckworth wrote in a post on X. “As Aviation Subcommittee Ranking Member, I’ll be demanding answers from the FAA,” she added. The disruption is the latest sign of strain on the US air traffic control system, which has ⁠been beset by equipment failures, communications problems and ⁠shortages of controllers, as the FAA tries to replace ageing infrastructure. Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company behind the FAA’s AI-powered air traffic management system, said its technology was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop. Travellers wait at Dallas Fort Worth international airport in Texas on November 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide [Tony Gutierrez/AP] “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a post on X. The FAA awarded ASI an $875m contract in June to develop and deploy the SMART system, which uses artificial intelligence to support air traffic management. The agency announced an expansion of the system across its 22 air traffic control centres on November 10, just days before the nationwide flight suspension. US rail service affected Amtrak, the US national rail operator, announced that its website and app are showing error messages and that customers are having difficulty reaching a representative, as it faces higher-than-normal call volumes because of the nationwide disruption to air travel. “We apologize for the error messages on both our website and app, as well as the difficulty reaching a representative,” Amtrak said in a post on X in response to a complaint. “We’re currently experiencing higher-than-normal call volumes due to ongoing airline issues,” the company said. It recommended that customers try the services later. Passengers wait as flights are delayed inside a terminal at Seattle-Tacoma international airport on November 13, 2026, in Seattle, Washington [Lindsey Wasson/AP] Pilot and former FAA safety team representative Kyle Bailey told Al Jazeera: “Whether you are an expert or not, the bottom line is we’re still trying to piece the puzzle together, and it would be impossible to have an answer to the issue quickly, in a few hours at least.” “But it is very alarming what we saw, and possibly [rail operator] Amtrak is being affected too,” he added. “The FAA’s priority at the moment is keeping not only the American passenger safe, but everyone flying in the US flight system.” Bailey said that “halting the flights on the ground is the safest thing to do until they could figure out what’s going on. If anybody says they think they know what’s causing this problem at such an early stage, they’re not being honest”. Congress approved $12.5bn for the overhaul last year, and the Department of Transportation and the White House asked lawmakers on Friday for ⁠another $30.1bn. This was the first nationwide US ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last time had been after the September 11, 2001, attacks. US authorities have yet to determine the cause of the telecommunications outage that prompted the ground stop.

items.title: Pakistan urges Gulf de-escalation as US, Iran trade accusations at UN
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan on Friday called for an immediate end to military provocations in the Gulf and renewed regional diplomacy as the United States, Iran and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries exchanged sharply conflicting accusations at a UN Security Council meeting on attacks against shipping and threats to maritime security. The debate highlighted growing concerns that the confrontation could disrupt international trade, energy supplies and food shipments while increasing the risk of a wider regional conflict. Addressing the Council, Pakistan’s Permanent Representative, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah , condemned attacks against Gulf countries and called for respect for their sovereignty and territorial integrity, protection of civilians and commercial shipping, and restoration of normal maritime traffic. He specifically condemned Houthi militia attacks and threats against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting civilian infrastructure and vessels engaged in lawful trade. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity. Highlighting the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandab Strait, Ambassador Shah warned that threats to maritime navigation endangered seafarers, disrupted international commerce and worsened energy and food insecurity, particularly in vulnerable economies. He called for the protection of commercial vessels and their crews, respect for freedom of navigation and safe, unimpeded delivery of humanitarian supplies. Lasting peace, he said, required addressing the underlying causes of regional conflicts through a framework based on common security, peaceful coexistence and mutual prosperity. He urged all parties to end attacks, maintain communication channels and support diplomatic initiatives, including the UN secretary-general’s good offices. The United States and Iran offered sharply contrasting accounts of the crisis, each blaming the other for the growing threats to maritime security. Iranian Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi accused Western members of the Council of ignoring the origins of the confrontation and attempting to reverse the roles of aggressor and victim. He identified what he described as unprovoked wars launched by the United States and Israel on June 13, 2025, and February 28, 2026 , as the root causes of the current insecurity. Recalling the attacks on Iran, he said they violated international law and targeted the country’s supreme leader, government officials, nuclear scientists and civilian infrastructure. He put the Iranian death toll at 5,000, including 254 children, and described the attacks as war crimes and crimes against humanity. “The insecurity surrounding the Strait of Hormuz is a direct consequence of these acts,” Ambassador Darzi said. While insisting that Iran remained committed to peace in the Persian Gulf, he argued that the presence of foreign military forces was itself a major source of instability and a threat to maritime safety. He rejected Security Council Resolution 2817 (2026), calling it politically motivated and accusing it of ignoring the origins of the crisis, denying Iran’s right to self-defence and failing to identify those responsible for the aggression. Tehran had not closed the door to diplomacy, he said, but Washington must end its military actions, provide credible guarantees against their repetition and lift what he called unlawful coercive measures against Iran. The US representative, Ambassador Jennifer Locetta, presented a sharply different picture, accusing Iran of aggression against its neighbours and threats to international shipping. “The regime attacks its neighbors, fires on commercial ships, arms terrorist proxies, and defies this Council at every turn,” she said. Iranian missiles, drones and what she described as unlawful mines in the Strait of Hormuz, along with attacks in the Bab el-Mandab Strait, threatened global energy and food security. Citing Security Council Resolution 2817 , which demanded that Iran stop attacks on shipping and neighbouring states and had attracted 136 co-sponsors, she said Tehran was defying the international community. “Iran ignores this Council. It ignores the overwhelming opinion of the international community,” she said. Ambassador Locetta also accused the Houthis of attacking Saudi airports and energy installations with Iranian backing and imposing an illegal, self-declared embargo on maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandab Strait. She said the group’s actions violated Security Council resolutions, including Resolution 2216 (2015), and urged Council members to hold Iran accountable. The GCC presented its own account of the attacks against its member states. Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said Gulf countries had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since February 28, targeting airports, ports, oil and gas facilities, power stations, water desalination plants and residential neighbourhoods. The attacks had caused deaths and injuries, extensive damage to property and infrastructure, and serious environmental repercussions in the Arabian Gulf, he said. Describing the strikes as flagrant violations of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of GCC members, Mr Albudaiwi said they threatened international peace and security and required Security Council action to ensure they stopped and were not repeated. Earlier, speaking on behalf of the GCC, Bahrain’s Ambassador Jamal Fares Alrowaiei welcomed mediation efforts by Oman, Qatar and Pakistan and reaffirmed the bloc’s commitment to diplomacy and de-escalation. “The security of the GCC States is indivisible,” he said, insisting that Gulf countries must participate in any negotiations concerning regional security. The competing positions underscored the difficulty of securing a diplomatic settlement, despite growing concern over the wider consequences of continued attacks and restrictions on shipping. The debate centred on restoring freedom of navigation, ending attacks on commercial vessels and civilian infrastructure, protecting seafarers and ensuring humanitarian access. Speakers also stressed the need for mediation, including efforts to facilitate US-Iran talks, and a negotiated settlement of broader regional and nuclear-related disputes. Pakistan reiterated its commitment to working with Gulf countries and international partners to promote de-escalation, maritime security and lasting regional peace and stability.
