items.title: How to Land 4,000 Planes During a Ground Stop
items.description: For four and a half hours, the sky above the United States emptied out. Normally, throughout the day and the night, thousands of planes are taking off, crisscrossing the country, and landing. When the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights around 4:00 p.m. today, because of “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” some 4,000 airplanes were in the sky, headed for U.S. airports, according to Flightradar24, an aviation-tracking website. Even if no more flights took off, all of those planes needed to land. For the people below, getting them down safely became an immediate preoccupation. This type of nationwide grounding had happened only twice before in recent history—once after the September 11 attacks, and once in January 2023 for about an hour and a half. Every aircraft still aloft needed to make it to its destination, despite apparently spotty communications. Our formidable system of flight, a machine that’s constantly in motion and choreographed to the minute, has backups built in. Pilots have emergency systems they can rely on if they lose radio communications, as well as onboard systems to detect where other aircraft are around them, R. John Hansman, the director of the MIT International Center for Air Transportation, told me. Communications problems don’t generally mean an immediate safety risk, and planes can still fly toward their destinations, he said. “The problem is getting them safely down.” “The risk is related to how many other airplanes you could bump into,” he said. “So if you stop putting new airplanes into the system, then it becomes safer and safer and safer, until there’s no airplanes in the air. But of course, nobody’s flying, right?” At the moment that the ground stop was declared, planes would have been landing. They landed in the minutes afterward, and in the hours after that. Within three hours, the number of flights still in the air had dropped to 550, Ian Petchenik, a spokesperson for Flightradar24, told me. Wheels hit the ground; the people on the plane and the people tracking their flights exhaled; pilots offered reassurances from the cockpit. On a plane that landed in Austin, carrying a number of writers headed a book festival (including some of my Atlantic colleagues), the pilot explained the delay on the tarmac by telling passengers there had been a “little issue with the FAA, folks, so no one is taking off and so there are no gates free.” In the first hours, the Trump administration offered little immediate reassurance, or clarification of what had gone wrong or how long it might take to fix. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.” More than four hours after the outage began, Mullin told reporters at the White House that “we have seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack” but also did not rule it out or explain a cause for the outage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who was on an airplane from Dallas amid the ground stop, said at the press conference that the country’s air traffic controllers faced “instability” in communications and radar—that switches and routers “actually got overwhelmed with data.” He blamed old analog equipment and software, and demanded $50 billion from Congress to fix the system. “It’s going to continue to fail,” he said. Some of the problems, Duffy said, affected communications with the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, a network of 22 regional hubs. Airplanes communicate with these centers as they fly across the country. The disruption also affected what are known as Terminal Radar Approach Controls, facilities where air traffic controllers help guide planes approaching and departing airports. During this outage, air traffic controllers could apparently communicate on some radio frequencies but not others, and they had to actively search for ways to talk with the airplanes in the sky, Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told CNN. “This is not just a bad day,” he said. The air traffic controllers were “handling something that’s never been seen before.” As the hours dragged on and planes kept landing but not taking off, the airports got crowded. Thousands of flights across the country got canceled. Passengers waited for hours, trying to figure out new plans, and scrambled for rental cars. They went home, or back to their hotels. Good Samaritans on social media offered rides. At Ronald Reagan National Airport, just outside Washington, D.C., hundreds of grounded travelers waited around a baggage carousel that moved so rarely that people felt comfortable sitting directly on it. Dana Johannesson, an ultrasound specialist in black scrubs and gold hoops, had gotten on her plane then gotten off, before waiting for her bags for hours; while she had sat on the plane, the American Airlines app still attributed the delay to the weather, but the pilot got on the loudspeaker to say that a friend had told him to give up on flying into Tampa and book himself a rental, she said. Then the ground stop lifted at 8:15 p.m. Thousands of planes that had been flying four hours earlier had landed. But fewer than 400 were still in the air. The passengers on those planes got on and off their plane as planned. The system started up again, and the planes could take off. Hana Kiros contributed reporting.

items.title: Estados Unidos reanuda el tráfico aéreo después de un parón de más de cuatro horas y 6.000 vuelos cancelados
items.description: Los aeropuertos de Estados Unidos vivieron este viernes una jornada caótica. items.title: Snowfall strands passengers, cargo at Khunjerab
items.description: GILGIT: Heavy snowfall and rain continued to cause hardships for residents of Gilgit-Baltistan on Friday, leaving a large number of passengers, tourists, vehicles and cargo containers stranded at Khunjerab Pass on the Pakistan-China border. Three containers reportedly skidded off the Karakoram Highway (KKH) after the road became slippery. Their drivers were rescued. Gilgit-Baltistan Minister for Tourism Naiknaam Karim was also among the stranded passengers and expressed concern over the lack of facilities and machinery to clear snow on the Pakistani side. A GB police official told Dawn that snowfall was continuing at Khunjerab Top, leaving several vehicles and dozens of containers carrying imported goods from China stranded for hours. In a press release, the GB police spokesperson said heavy snowfall was continuing from Dhee Headquarters to Khunjerab Top, while accumulated snow had made the road hazardous for travel. Tourists and travellers were advised to avoid unnecessary journeys and refrain from travelling towards Khunjerab until weather and road conditions improved. Stranded passengers complained that the government and relevant organisations had not started clearing the road for traffic. The police spokesperson said a Chinese container had overturned after skidding on the snow-covered road. Local travellers and personnel of the Khunjerab Security Police launched a rescue operation and safely pulled the driver out of the vehicle. He remained unhurt. Motorists were advised to avoid unnecessary travel during heavy snowfall and contact the police helpline at 15 before setting out to obtain the latest information about road conditions. The stranded passengers said the area, situated at an altitude of over 15,000 feet, posed additional difficulties because of the risk of oxygen shortage and other problems. In a video message, Minister Naiknaam Karim said snowfall had also occurred on the Chinese side, but the road had been cleared for traffic. “However, after entering the Pakistani side, we found the road at Khunjerab Top covered with approximately four inches of snow and ice. Several vehicles, including two to three cars, have skidded due to slippery road conditions,” he said. He regretted that the road had not been cleared and appealed to the Frontier Works Organisation (FWO) to immediately deploy machinery to prevent further accidents. Meanwhile, the Ghizer-Shandur Road was completely blocked to all types of traffic following a landslide at Hopper Pari after heavy rain on Thursday night. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: Fazl’s son skips another summons from NAB in Pakistan post case
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Asad Meh­­mood, son of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Reh­­man, on Friday skipped the second notice issued by the National Accountabi­li­­ty Bureau (NAB) and did not appear before its investigation team in a case involving alleged irregularities in appointments during his tenure as a federal minister in 2022-23. A source in the bureau told Dawn that as Asad Mehmood had not complied with the first notice issued on Nov 10, the NAB Rawalpindi/Islamabad Regional Office had served him a second notice, asking him to appear before its team on Friday. “How­ever, Asad Mehmood def­ied the second summons and did not visit the NAB office,” the source added. According to sources, the anti-graft watchdog will soon serve a third notice on the former minister and, in case he ignores it, NAB could take stern action, including his arrest. In such cases, NAB usually serves second and third notices on the accused and, if all three are ignored, the anti-graft watchdog takes punitive action, including the arrest of the accused. Under the NAB notice, Asad Mehmood was req­uired to appear before the investigators to explain his position on alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments at Pakistan Post during his 2022-23 tenure as federal minister. Asad Mehmood had served as a federal minister during the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM) government in 2022-23. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: COP31 : le front du "pollueur-payeur" donne de la voix
items.description: De la colère des militants réclamant des réparations aux négociations ardues sur des centaines de milliards de dollars, la question du financement a cristallisé toutes les tensions, ce vendredi 13 novembre 2026, lors de la Conférence des Nations unies sur le climat (COP31) à Antalya, en Turquie. Au cœur des échanges : la fracture profonde entre les responsabilités historiques des grandes puissances émettrices et la vulnérabilité financière des pays du Sud. Dans les travées du sommet turc, le message des organisations de la société civile s'est résumé à un mot d’ordre unanime : « Faites payer les pollueurs » et « Annulation de la dette ». Une exigence incarnée par le témoignage d'un militant nigérian qui, évoquant l'assèchement du lac Tchad et les déplacements de populations qu'il engendre, a dénoncé les taux d'intérêt prohibitifs imposés aux pays en développement pour financer leur survie climatique, là où les nations riches empruntent à bas coût. En conférence de presse, le Secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a dressé un constat alarmant sur l'ampleur des besoins financiers. « Même en triplant les financements pour l’adaptation, on ne couvrirait pas 30 % des besoins réels », a-t-il dit. Soulignant que les chocs climatiques annulent des décennies de progrès économiques et replongent les populations dans la précarité, il a plaidé pour une taxation des superprofits des majors des énergies fossiles et une refonte de l'architecture financière internationale issue de l'après-Seconde Guerre mondiale. Selon lui, une réforme de la gouvernance des banques multilatérales permettrait un effet de levier majeur, chaque dollar investi pouvant générer entre huit et dix dollars de financements. Un diagnostic partagé par le patron d'ONU Climat, Simon Stiell, qui a mis en garde contre le cercle vicieux liant catastrophes naturelles et surendettement. Alors que l'objectif global de financement atteint 1 300 milliards de dollars par an — dont au moins 300 milliards mobilisés par les pays développés d'ici 2035 —, la trajectoire actuelle laisse présager un déficit annuel abyssal de 840 milliards. Pour tenter de réduire cet écart, des institutions financières du Royaume-Uni, de Norvège et du Canada ont annoncé une initiative conjointe visant à mobiliser 10 milliards de dollars d'ici 2030 en faveur des marchés émergents. Sécurité alimentaire et assurances paramétriques : l'urgence de l'adaptation Au-delà des grands équilibres macrofinanciers, les experts présents à Antalya ont alerté sur le sous-financement chronique des secteurs vitaux. Kaveh Zahedi, de l’Organisation des Nations unies pour l’alimentation et l’agriculture (FAO), a déploré que l’agriculture ne capte qu’environ 5 % des financements climatiques liés au développement, une part en recul constant malgré l'aggravation des phénomènes météorologiques comme El Niño. « Le plus grand risque, c’est de ne pas investir dans l’agriculture, car on s’expose alors à une aggravation de la faim » , a-t-il prévenu. Pour accélérer le versement des aides en cas de sinistre, l'assurance dite « paramétrique » s'impose comme un levier prometteur. Déployé dans huit États du Pacifique — où il a déjà bénéficié à des dizaines de milliers d'habitants, notamment aux Fidji —, ce mécanisme déclenche des indemnisations automatiques dès qu'un seuil météorologique prédéfini (vitesse des vents, niveau de précipitations) est franchi, évitant ainsi les délais interminables d'expertise des dégâts. Comme le souligne Sinja Buri, de l’Université des Nations unies, la rapidité du décaissement conditionne directement le coût et la durée du relèvement économique. Parallèlement, des acteurs de terrain ont défendu la rentabilité économique de la transition écologique à l'échelle locale. Hunter Lovins, fondatrice de l’ONG Natural Capitalism Solutions, a illustré la résilience offerte par l'autonomie énergétique — évoquant sa propre habitation solaire restée alimentée durant une semaine d'inondations dans le Colorado — tout en appelant les citoyens des 57 pays mobilisés par son réseau à agir sans attendre l'impulsion des États. L'adieu combatif d'António Guterres aux sommets climatiques Cette journée a également été marquée par un moment d’intense émotion lors d’une rencontre entre António Guterres et les représentants de la société civile, venus saluer le Secrétaire général à l’occasion de sa dernière COP en fonction. Acclamé par une longue ovation debout et décoré d'un prix symbolique intitulé « Faites payer les pollueurs », le chef de l'ONU a appelé les militants à maintenir la pression face à l'influence des lobbys des énergies fossiles sur les gouvernements. S'il quitte bientôt la tête des Nations unies, António Guterres a assuré qu'il « ne cessera pas de se battre » pour la justice climatique. The post COP31 : le front du "pollueur-payeur" donne de la voix appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Balochistan Assembly seeks compulsory Arabic in primary schools
items.description: QUETTA: The Balochistan Assembly on Friday unanimously adopted a resolution recommending the introduction of basic Arabic as a compulsory subject in all government primary schools across the province. The resolution was moved by JUI-F MPA Shahida Rauf, who said teaching basic Arabic would help students understand commonly used Quranic words and their meanings, enabling them to develop a better understanding of the Holy Quran from an early age. The resolution called for a simple, standardised and grade-wise curriculum covering basic Arabic vocabulary, grammar and commonly used Quranic expressions. It also stressed the need for trained teachers, quality textbooks, appropriate teaching materials and effective monitoring. It recommended that the provincial government introduce the initiative through a phased programme, taking into account students’ ages, mental abilities and educational needs, with regular reviews of its implementation. During the discussion, MPA Dr Abdul Malik Baloch recalled that legislation had been passed in 2013 to promote education in mother languages. He urged the government to implement that law alongside the proposed Arabic language programme. Following the discussion, the Assembly unanimously approved the resolution, recommending the introduction of compulsory basic Arabic education in government primary schools throughout Balochistan. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: Scenes From the Nationwide Ground Stop
items.description: On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare ground stop at all U.S. airports, citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” Across the country, departing flights were held for hours before the stop—attributed to a telecommunications outage—was lifted, disrupting travel plans for some 1.5 million people. As planes start to take off again, thousands of passengers are still stuck on the ground. items.title: Act now on El Nino or pay double later, UNDP chief warns
items.description: • Delay could push global price tag from $36bn to $73bn; De Croo urges IMF, wealthy nations to back crisis-hit economies • China reportedly rules out hosting 2028 COP33 climate summit ANTALYA: Act now against the devastating effects of El Nino or pay double later, the head of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) warned on Friday as delegates debated how to finance climate action at the COP31 talks in Turkey. “The needs to hedge the impact of El Nino are $36 billion if you do it now,” the agency’s chief, Alexander De Croo, said in an interview in the Turkish resort of Antalya. “If you don’t do it, the cost will be $73bn. So the cost would be two times as high.” El Nino heats Pacific Ocean waters every two to seven years, disrupting global wind patterns and rainfall. This exceptionally strong cycle has already battered economies worldwide. “Not acting is the most expensive climate policy that you could have,” De Croo warned, urging major players such as the International Monetary Fund to help vulnerable developing nations mitigate the damage. Developing countries want more financial support from wealthier nations historically responsible for global warming, though De Croo acknowledged rich governments face heavy debt burdens and war costs. Still, he argued vulnerable nations have had no time to recover from compounding crises: the Covid-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, “and now El Nino, and now the cost of financing”. A UN report this week noted African Development Bank estimates of $10bn to $20bn in regional damage, while the UN Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean projected cumulative GDP losses of at least 2pc over three years, pushing 4.8 million people into poverty. While De Croo pressed for immediate adaptation investments and policy reforms to lower capital costs across 47 partner nations, questions over long-term global climate leadership also surfaced on the sidelines of the Antalya summit. Separately, China has decided against hosting the UN’s annual climate talks in 2028 after considering the possibility in recent months, sources familiar with the issue said Friday on condition of anonymity at COP31. Beijing’s decision leaves the door open for another Asia-Pacific nation to organise COP33, as it is the region’s turn to host. India withdrew its offer in April without specifying a reason, while South Korea has previously expressed interest. Asked about the decision, first reported by The Guardian, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said he was unaware of the situation, adding that China remains committed to “promoting the global green and low-carbon transition”. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President’s son fuels Ugandan succession fever
items.description: In Uganda’s military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country’s powerful army chief. Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military’s top ranks. The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades. Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party. This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position. The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as “completely false”. This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general’s presidential ambitions. Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account. At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures. A recent meeting of NRM’s top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni’s successor, according to the AFP news agency. Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal. Uganda’s news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general’s potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership. In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss “political, social and economic issues”. He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda’s next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions “through the right channel, at the right time”. President Yoweri Museveni’s grandson (standing up, shaking the president’s hand) has joined the army, alongside his father (sitting down, wearing camouflage) Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada’s York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni’s succession, often referred to as the “Muhoozi Project”. “Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason,” he tells the BBC. He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question. Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general’s forgiveness. The detention of one of the country’s most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu , has brought the crackdown into sharper focus. The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region. His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted. “The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private,” Kainerugaba wrote on X. He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested. The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post. The army later confirmed Elwelu’s detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations. Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda’s Daily Monitor newspaper. They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda’s most sensitive security operations.Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption. He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had “forgiven” him. Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor. His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him. Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications. The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces. Maj Gen James Birungi was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge. He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive. “Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief,” Egesa says, adding: “The arrests are not summarily done.” But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba’s presidential ambitions are being targeted. “The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi,” he says. He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president’s son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession. The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released. Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings. “Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice,” he adds. He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba. Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as “hogwash”. Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy. On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job. “Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon,” he wrote, in posts that he later deleted. He also questioned Alupo’s loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate “on military terms”, if he became his father’s deputy. The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible. It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it. Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly. Vice-President Jessica Alupo is yet to respond to Gen Kainerugaba’s posts questioning her loyalty Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba’s controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda’s political and military stability. Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics. He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party. Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations. Under Uganda’s military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army. Bareebe argues that the SFC’s loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power. “The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son,” he adds. At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war. He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year , extending his rule into a fifth decade. Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father’s current term is due to end. He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership. But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated. At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported. Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni’s younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership. There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president. Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation. Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion. He suggests Museveni’s reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition. “The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition,” he says. The military has been central to Museveni’s hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify. The family’s military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba’s son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain’s Sandhurst military academy. The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition. Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies. Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year’s presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba . The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability. For now, Museveni remains in power. But the arrests, his son’s threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda’s next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

items.title: COP31 must deliver climate justice, not empty pledges, says Sherry
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Senator Sherry Rehman Friday called for COP31 in Antalya to move beyond declarations and deliver a credible, accessible and equitable climate financing framework, warning that Pakistan and other climate-vulnerable countries were being pushed into a dangerous cycle of disasters, debt and declining development opportunities. In a statement issued here on Friday, Senator Rehman expressed her appreciation for Turkiye’s hosting of COP31 and its Presidency of this critical global climate conference, recognising Turkiye’s role in bringing the international community together at a time of growing geopolitical divisions and escalating climate emergencies. “Pakistan deeply appreciates Turkiye’s leadership in hosting COP31. As a close friend and longstanding partner, Turkiye understands the devastating human and economic costs of climate disasters. Its Presidency offers an important opportunity to bridge divisions between developed and developing countries and restore confidence in multilateral climate action. “We hope the Antalya conference will be remembered not simply for renewed pledges, but for translating climate solidarity into concrete fina­ncial commitments and meaningful outcomes for vulnerable nations.” Referring to the UN Secretary-General’s address at the COP31 Leaders’ Summit, where he warned that “fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs”, Senator Rehman stressed that the world could no longer afford the contradiction between climate commitments and continued support for fossil fuels. “Governments cannot continue subsidising the very industries driving the climate crisis while pleading scarcity of resources when vulnerable countries demand climate fina­nce. Global fossil fuel subsidies are estimated at approximately $7 trillion. “This is an extraordinary misallocation of resources at a time when countries on the climate frontlines are struggling to finance basic adaptation, resilience and recovery. The question is not whether the world has the resources, but whether it has the political will to redirect them,” Senator Rehman said. She warned that the global temperature trajectory was becoming increasingly alarming, with the 1.5°C goal slipping further out of reach. According to Climate Action Tracker, current policies put the world on course for approximately 2.7 degrees centigrade of warming by the end of the century, up from its previous estimate of 2.6 degrees centigrade. “The 1.5 degrees centigrade thre­shold is no longer alive, a 2.7 degrees centigrade trajectory would have devastating consequences for countries like Pakistan, where climate extremes are already undermining livelihoods, food security, water availability and economic stability. “The cost of inaction will be measured in lost lives, displaced communities and development reversed by decades.” Highlighting Pakistan’s escalating climate vulnerability, Senator Rehman recalled that the devastating floods of 2022 affected 33 million people and caused approximately $30 billion in damages and losses. Agricultural losses from the 2025 floods alone have been estimated at $1 billion. “These are not isolated disasters. They represent a recurring assault on Pakistan’s economy, food security, infrastructure and development prospects. Pakistan is not asking for charity. We are demanding climate justice, financial accountability and a fair international system,” she said. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: Yemeni govt forces fortify defences in Aden
items.description: ABU DHABI: Yemen’s internationally recognised government is fortifying positions on the outskirts of Aden province, home to their de facto capital, as their Houthi foes seize hilltops overlooking the area, military officials told AFP. Fighting has flared since a 2022 truce fell apart over the summer, with violence intensifying after Yemen’s Saudi-backed government lost control of the Red Sea coastline along the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in September. The Houthis are now advancing east, consolidating their gains near the Red Sea while also moving closer to the Gulf of Aden. They have been taking hold of strategic hilltops in the Al-Madaribah wal Ara district overlooking Aden province, the sources said. “We received high-level directives to establish military fortifications west and north of Aden Governorate, as the threat to the government’s interim capital draws nearer,” one of the military officials said. The fortifications inc­lude stacking up sandbags and digging tunnels. All the sources req­uested anonymity to discuss sensitive matters. Government forces have repeatedly tried to regain control of the Red Sea coast to no avail, with battles killing dozens on both sides in the past couple of days, according to government and Houthi sources. Another of the military officials described the fortification outside Aden as a long-overdue precautionary measure. The third military sou­rce, a field officer on the ground, said the Hou­this were advancing east of the strait towards the Gulf of Aden coast after taking large parts of Al-Madaribah wal Ara district. Nearby also lies the region of Al-Maqatirah, home to a road serving as the main gateway to Taiz, which has been besieged by the Houthis for weeks. The source said Al-Maqatirah had been captured by Houthis, complicating government efforts to retake Taiz and opening the door to further advances in Al-Madaribah. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: A Reader’s Perspective on Federalism, Insecurity, and the Pursuit of an Own Ethnic Region in Southern Ethiopia
items.description: A book chapter by Beza Dessalegn entitled “Federalism, Insecurity, and the Pursuit of an Own Ethnic Region in Southern Ethiopia” in the book Ethiopia’s Insecurity Complex: Protest, Transition and War , published in 2025 examines the under researched direct relationship between federalism and security in Ethiopia. The chapter analyses the pre- and post-2018 quest for regional statehood and the securitized responses of the federal and regional governments to these demands. It situates its analysis within the framework of “emerging anarchy,” exploring the relationship between Ethiopia’s federal structure and security in the context of rising demands for autonomy. Given the book chapter addresses the historical-comparative political development of the pre-and post-2018 regional statehood claims and state response, and the national dialogue process that might rethink the whole state structure arrangement, the review would contribute to an ongoing discussion on federal structure, social cohesions and state building. Using the former Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples’ (SNNP) Region as a case study, the chapter argues that both the creation and disintegration of the region were driven by political competition among dominant ethnic groups, as well as the pursuit of identity, self-determination, and regional autonomy by constituent ethnic communities. The main argument of the chapter is that the federal system, which was supposed to advocate for ensuring self-rule, has been challenged by the rising demands for self-rule. This is further challenged by the inconsistent granting of regional status and the securitized responses of the federal and regional governments. These demands in turn came to be perceived as threats to regime security and the continuity of the federation as a whole. The government’s perception of such demands as threats to regime security and national unity was evident both before and after the 2018 political development. This perception is not an isolated scene rather it is grounded in the broken promises, historical grievances, and the longstanding historical relationship among groups and with the state. The book chapter also raise the fact that these demands are rooted in the historical relationship and power dynamics, manifesting as both horizontal and vertical insecurity. The chapter further claims the lack of institutional mechanisms that can sufficiently tackle differences without it leading to violence. However, the formation of the regional state appears to have excluded minorities within regions from political rights perpetuating erosion of societal cohesion. On the other hand, the chapter frames the role played by political elites in weaponising ethnicity to materialize displacements, without any accountability, within the layers of security threats and insecurity patterns. However, the book chapter gave less emphasis to the discussion of institutional responses especially in their lack of capacity, tokenistic approach and domino effect. The institutional response inadequacy can be attested by the Administrative Boundaries and Identity Issues Commission’s conclusion that the majority of residents preferred the continuity of the SNNP region despite the widespread violence, and reports of threats and calls for the expulsion of the region’s ethnic minorities from their regions. This can also be taken as a lesson for institutions/commission with defect in their nature or performance. Finally, the chapter is being reviewed amid the convening of the National Dialogue, which has proposed shifting the authorship of the FDRE constitution to “the people of multinational Ethiopia” and granting the federal government a broader mandate to intervene in regions experiencing conflicts presumed to constitute emergencies. This context adds another dimension to the chapter’s analysis: a legalized unsolicited federal intervention could produce unintended consequences for the balance between regional autonomy and state consolidation particularly if what constitutes “ internal conflict of an emergency nature ” is not clearly predefined. This is especially relevant to the chapter’s conclusion on the need for a proactive response, inclusive governance, and a human-centered approach. Disclaimer: The views expressed in this Insight reflect the perspectives of the contributor and do not necessarily represent the official position of Institute for Peace and Security Studies. Contributed by Haymanot Kassahun Programme Officer The post A Reader’s Perspective on Federalism, Insecurity, and the Pursuit of an Own Ethnic Region in Southern Ethiopia appeared first on IPSS .

items.title: Mfantsipim’s red-and-black uniform: How student indiscipline created a school identity
items.description: What is now one of Mfantsipim School’s most recognisable symbols was born out of an attempt to deal with student indiscipline. The school’s distinctive red-and-black striped shirt, worn with black shorts, was introduced in 2009 after some students reportedly sneaked out of the campus and, when confronted in town, denied they attended Mfantsipim. The explanation they gave was that they were students of a nearby institution, CSI, whose peach tops and khaki shorts closely resembled Mfantsipim’s uniform at the time. That similarity made it difficult to identify the boys, prompting the school authorities to seek a new design that would set Mfantsipim students apart. The decision eventually produced a uniform that has become a source of pride for generations of students and old boys, and a prominent feature of the school’s 150th anniversary celebrations this year. The change was initiated by the then headmaster, Mr Koame Nieza Edjah, who tasked the school’s Art Department with coming up with a new design. A graphic design teacher and old boy, Ishmael Mcanslan Mensah, worked with students to develop several proposals. A committee subsequently settled on the red-and-black striped shirt and black shorts, which have remained the school’s distinctive attire. The change was not merely about appearance. It was also intended to make it easier for school authorities and members of the public to identify Mfantsipim students outside the campus, particularly when disciplinary issues arose. A tribute to the school’s pioneers The colours were chosen to carry a deeper meaning, linking the students of today to the men whose efforts helped establish the institution. The red represents the blood shed by the school’s founding fathers in their struggle to establish the school, while black honours the Black race. The design pays tribute to prominent figures associated with the school’s beginnings, including Kwabena Sekyi, John Mensah Sarbah and J.C. Brown. A Ghana News Agency report published in June 2009, when the new uniform was unveiled, also recorded the explanation that the colours were intended to honour the founding fathers and give the school a distinct identity. The then headmaster, identified in that report as Mr Koame Nieza Edjah, said the uniform represented a new vision, character and attitude for the institution. The red-and-black outfit has since become inseparable from the image of the school. It is popularly associated with the nickname “Kotokuraba AC Milan”, a playful reference to the colours of the Italian football club. 150 years of Mfantsipim The uniform’s story is receiving renewed attention as Mfantsipim marks 150 years of existence in 2026. Founded on April 3, 1876, in Cape Coast by the Wesleyan Mission, the school began as Wesleyan High School with 17 students and James Picot as its first headmaster. It is recognised as the first second-cycle school established in the then Gold Coast. Over the years, the institution has produced prominent personalities in politics, law, education, business, religion and other fields, earning a reputation as one of Ghana’s most influential schools. The sesquicentennial celebrations, themed “A Legacy of Excellence, Leadership and Service to Inspire the Future”, have included the unveiling of commemorative anniversary cloth and official songs, as well as activities to recognise the school’s contribution to national development. What began as a practical response to students slipping out of school has therefore taken on a significance its designers may not have anticipated. The uniform now represents discipline, history and a shared identity for the Mfantsipim community. As the school celebrates its 150th year, the red-and-black stripes remain a visible reminder of its past and the generations of students who have carried its name.

items.title: The Next Major Grounding Will Be Worse
items.description: Call me Dumb Nostradamus. Two days ago, I was on my friend Pablo Torre’s podcast to discuss some of my recent reporting on artificial intelligence. A lot of accomplished cybersecurity people I’ve spoken with are convinced that the combination of rapidly advancing AI systems, the diffusion of those systems via open-source models, and the rickety state of the world’s software will lead to something like rolling waves of chaos. Paraphrasing those experts, I told Pablo, “There’s going to be stuff that doesn’t work that disrupts your daily lives—and that’s the best you can hope for.” That I learned all domestic flights in the United States were being grounded minutes after my own flight this evening landed—safely, and with the country’s chillest passengers and Delta crew—just goes to show that predicting chaos and being prepared for it are two very different skills. To be clear, I have no idea what caused this. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed a communications issue for interfering with air traffic control. It could be a classic software-upgrade face-palm; the extremely rare ground stop coincided with the FAA’s recent rollout of SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories), an $875 million AI-enhanced air-traffic-management system. The system’s maker, Air Space Intelligence, denies that its technology was at fault. Of course, the stop also coincided with yesterday’s Microsoft Outlook outage. That’s a lot of cyber smoke in two days. Even if today has a boring explanation, the experts I’ve been talking with are pretty sure that plenty of days like this are coming, for two main reasons. [ Ian Bogost: Airport chaos began long before the ground stop ] First, anyone can be a bad guy now. Switching off a country’s power grid has technically been possible for a long time. What stopped anyone was the logic that kept the Cold War cold. The only people capable of that kind of chaos were governments, and governments know that turning off another country’s lights is exactly the sort of thing that gets answered with missiles. Deterrence works on parties who have something to lose and an address where you can send a reply. The trouble with AI (um, one of the troubles) is that it may hand state-grade capability to people who have neither. You can’t deter a vandal. You don’t know who he is, and he doesn’t care, and he may currently be eating cereal in a gaming chair. The kids who used to grab a bat and swing at mailboxes can now grab some compute and turn off a town’s refrigerators—not for money or a cause, but because why not? Historically, that’s been the motive behind a great deal of human mischief. Second, our best defense against this kind of chaos is amputation. None of the security people I’ve talked with has predicted an apocalypse. But they’re pretty convinced that the next 18 months are going to be a hassle, with regular disruptions to services that we rely on. That’s because when cyber defenders find a hole they can’t patch fast enough, the rational move is to amputate: Switch the system off and wait. Big institutions already do this, more quietly and more often than you’d think. Whatever caused today’s ground stop, halting every departure in the country “for reasons of safety” until someone works out what’s going on isn’t a sign that the system is failing. More and more, it is the system. I’ve just watched it from 22C. You can do some things to protect yourself, but they fall into the realm of flossing: Install the update when your phone nags you, use passkeys instead of text-message codes, keep a little cash and water around. There’s some safety in numbers. Gmail and your giant bank are obvious targets, but they also employ armies of very serious, very well-paid people whose whole job is looking for trouble. And if they go down, hey, we’ll all have problems big enough that the world reading your love letters and poring over your credit-card statement will be the least of them. The disorientation will be harder to adjust to. Most of us have been privileged to live in a world of peace, prosperity, and, above all, stability. We’ve gone to bed without having to wonder whether the traffic lights will work tomorrow. Now, if my sources are correct, we should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time, and the main skill you need is not being surprised.

items.title: Of Course Americans Blamed the Ground Stop on AI
items.description: For many hours, the Federal Aviation Administration did not explain why it issued a national ground stop in the United States this afternoon. The agency described the cause only as a “ telecommunications outage ” and cited “ extraordinary circumstances ,” but failed to say more. So speculation abounded: Was the problem connected with the onboarding of a new AI route-selection system this week? Is it somehow related to the Microsoft Outlook outage this week? Or is the cause some antiquated telecommunications system that just finally gave up trying? In the absence of solid information from trusted authorities, people interpret crises through the prism of their preexisting concerns. When the aviation system shut down, many Americans’ minds went to DOGE cuts, cyberattacks by hostile foreign actors, recent reports of renegade AI. A safety planner’s job is to envision the full range of possible threats and assess how likely each one is to occur. Even before recent advances in artificial intelligence, the list of factors that could jeopardize commercial aviation was already long: terrorism, extreme weather, staffing strains, the decay of outdated communications networks, and more. AI could theoretically help the aviation system manage risks and disruptions, but it also adds many more variables that could go wrong. It’s no wonder many Americans were quick to envision rogue disruption caused by the new technology: When AI CEOs tell us that the risk of AI is so great that it is essentially uninsurable, people take notice. The more prosaic reality is that America’s crucial infrastructure systems are built without sufficient resiliency. As a result, a single disruption can have national consequences. CNN reported tonight that the aviation problem may have originated with network routers at Chicago’s Midway airport. In a fragile system, glitches spread unpredictably and potentially rapidly. So far, more than 10,000 flights have been disrupted . Fortunately, our aviation-safety systems had sufficient backups to let planes land safely, and pilots have been communicating through emergency-frequency lines. The best analogy is a spare tire: It’s good enough to get you to the nearest gas station but not much farther. The ground stop—which has now been lifted—has exposed either a new security vulnerability or a problem with old systems; either way, the economic impact could well be major. The high stakes are all the more reason that, in moments of crisis, authorities should quickly tell the public what is known, what is not known, and what they are doing to close the information gap. Finally, after four hours, the Trump administration held a press conference, at which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that “things seem to be working, as we can say, in the right direction.” How long it will take for the mess at airports to clear is anyone’s guess.

items.title: Mahama boosts BNI with 111 new vehicles, state-of-the-art forensic lab and interrogation centre
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has officially presented a fleet of 111 operational vehicles and unveiled a newly established forensic laboratory and modernised interrogation centre for the Bureau of National Intelligence (BNI). The high-level commissioning ceremony, held in Accra, marks a major logistical and technological boost for Ghana’s premier intelligence agency, aimed at sharpening its operational readiness, investigative capacity, and response to contemporary security threats. Addressing officers and senior security heads, President Mahama emphasized that intelligence and investigations remain central to safeguarding national peace, noting that modern criminal syndicates require advanced digital tools and mobility to effectively counter. Focus on cybercrime and digital forensics Highlighting the inclusion of the state-of-the-art forensic facility, the President stressed that the laboratory will significantly enhance the BNI’s capability to probe complex cybercrimes, financial frauds, and other sophisticated digital offences. “The commissioning of this digital forensic laboratory is an important development in our collective efforts to investigate cybercrime and other sophisticated offences committed today,” President Mahama stated. The newly upgraded interrogation centre features advanced soundproofing and modern digital recording equipment designed to ensure transparent, accountable, and professional investigative procedures. Safeguarding human rights and dignity While challenging security personnel to maintain high standards of vigilance in keeping the nation safe, President Mahama charged operatives to uphold the fundamental rights and dignity of individuals brought in for questioning. He underscored that the physical environment of the renovated interrogation rooms must reflect a balance between rigorous state security and strict adherence to human rights, ensuring that suspects are treated appropriately while investigators execute their statutory mandates. The provision of the 111 vehicles is expected to ease mobility constraints across regional and district commands, ensuring rapid response deployment and seamless intelligence gathering nationwide. Security chiefs and invited dignitaries at the ceremony commended the government’s decisive retooling of the intelligence apparatus, viewing it as a pivotal milestone in strengthening national security architecture. This broadcast footage captures the official commissioning ceremony where President Mahama handed over the vehicles and inaugurated the new intelligence infrastructure.

items.title: Ghana targets homegrown AI solutions, not rivalry with US, China – Ato Forson
items.description: Ghana is looking to develop artificial intelligence (AI) tools that solve local problems rather than compete with the advanced technology industries of the United States and China, Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has said. He said the proposed National Artificial Intelligence Centre would concentrate on practical applications that could improve services and support professionals in key sectors, particularly healthcare. Dr Forson explained that the government was not seeking to build a system capable of matching the global technology giants but wanted Ghana to develop its own capacity to use AI to meet its needs. “We don’t intend to challenge China or America, but we want to modestly have our own AI system,” he said in an interview on the Citi Breakfast Show on Friday, November 13. He cited healthcare as one area where the technology could make a difference, saying doctors should be able to use AI tools to support their work. “The intention is to pay particular attention to certain models. Healthcare, for example. Doctors, for example, should be able to use artificial intelligence to assist them in their work, among other models,” he added. His comments offer further insight into the government’s plans for the proposed centre, which was announced in the 2027 Budget presented to Parliament on Thursday, November 12. Under the technology pillar of the government’s New Economy programme, an investment of US$300 million is planned between 2027 and 2028 to establish the centre and upgrade rural mobile networks from 2G to reliable 4G connectivity. The centre is expected to provide computing facilities, secure data environments, research laboratories and infrastructure for testing AI models. It will also offer professional training and support for start-ups. According to the budget, the facility will give Ghanaian businesses, universities, researchers and public institutions access to computing resources that would be too costly for many of them to acquire independently. Focus on local needs Healthcare is not the only sector expected to benefit from the initiative. The government has identified agriculture, energy, mining, logistics, Ghanaian languages and public services as areas for AI development. In agriculture, for instance, AI tools could help farmers access useful information and improve decision-making, while applications in public services could support the delivery of services and administrative processes. The emphasis on Ghanaian languages is also significant, as locally developed tools could help address the limitations of digital platforms that do not adequately serve people who communicate mainly in local languages. The budget also makes provision for practical training in software development, data analytics, artificial intelligence, computer networks and digital business services to prepare young people for jobs and business opportunities in the technology sector. Rural connectivity in the plan The planned upgrade of rural 2G networks to 4G is another major component of the investment. Presenting the budget, Dr Forson said improved connectivity would allow farmers to receive weather and market information, make digital payments and reach buyers. It would also enable rural health facilities to access telehealth services, students to use online learning materials and small businesses to reach customers beyond their communities. The government says the objective is to ensure that a person’s location does not prevent them from accessing modern digital services or participating in the emerging technology economy. The AI centre and network upgrade form part of the four-year US$10 billion New Economy programme, which will run from 2027 to 2030. The programme has eight priority areas, including commercial agriculture, energy infrastructure, value addition to critical minerals, tourism and creative arts, textiles and garments, pharmaceuticals and biomanufacturing, and the technology economy. Government has earmarked GH¢30 billion for the programme in 2027, representing 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product. The broader ambition is to expand domestic production, strengthen local industries and create jobs.

items.title: Le Moussem religieux et culturel de Moulay Abdellah Chérif, du 18 au 21 novembre à Ouezzane
items.description: Le Moussem religieux et culturel de Moulay Abdellah Chérif El Ouazzani se tiendra, du 18 au 21 novembre, sous le thème « Sur la voie prophétique… et dans un esprit d'unité : rayonnement spirituel et fidélité à la nation », à l'initiative de l’Association Dar Dmana chargée de la gestion des affaires de la zaouïa Ouazzania. Cet événement, organisé sous l'égide de la Zaouïa Ouazzania, en partenariat avec la préfecture de la province d'Ouazzane, le ministère de la Jeunesse, de la Culture et des Sports, la commune d'Ouazzane et le Conseil provincial d'Ouazzane, s'inscrit dans le cadre de la commémoration de la Fête de l'Unité, de la glorieuse Marche Verte et de la glorieuse Fête de l'Indépendance. Dans une note de présentation de l'événement, les organisateurs ont souligné que l'édition 2026 revêt une importance particulière, compte tenu du contexte national et religieux dans lequel elle se déroule, relevant qu'elle constitue l'occasion de mettre en avant les valeurs du Message prophétique fait de miséricorde, du juste milieu et de modération, à la lumière de l'Initiative Royale relative à la commémoration du quinzième centenaire de la naissance du Prophète (paix et salut soient sur Lui). La même source a ajouté que cette édition s'inscrit également dans un contexte national marqué par la dynamique que connaît la question de l'intégrité territoriale du Royaume, notamment suite à l'adoption de la résolution 2797 par le Conseil de sécurité des Nations Unies, ainsi que par l'évolution du débat international autour de l'initiative d'autonomie, désormais reconnue comme la seule base pour les négociations. Ce rendez-vous annuel vise à préserver la mémoire locale, à relier les nouvelles générations à leur héritage civilisationnel et spirituel, et à mettre en lumière le rôle historique des zaouïas marocaines dans l'ancrage des fondements religieux et nationaux, des valeurs de solidarité et de loyauté envers la patrie, ainsi que dans la contribution au développement local. Le programme de cet événement, dont l’ouverture officielle est prévue le 18 novembre sur la « Place de l’Aéroport », comprend un éventail d’activités à caractère religieux, scientifique, culturel et social. Sur le plan religieux et spirituel, le programme prévoit une matinée consacrée au Dikr, au Wird et à la lecture de « Dala'il al-Khayrat » au mausolée de Moulay Abdellah Chérif. Il inclut également un défilé des confréries et groupes soufis, partant du mausolée de Sidi Ali Ben Ahmed en direction de celui de Moulay Abdellah Chérif, ainsi que des soirées dédiées à la récitation du Coran, au Samaâ et au Madih à la Grande Mosquée, au Centre culturel et au mausolée de Moulay Touhami. Sur les plans intellectuel, artistique et patrimonial, le programme comprend une table ronde et un grand colloque scientifique au Centre culturel, l'inauguration d'une exposition d'artisanat et de produits du terroir, ainsi qu'une exposition d'arts plastiques au complexe artisanal. Le programme prévoit également des spectacles folkloriques et des exhibitions de Tbourida, ainsi qu’une grande soirée artistique dédiée aux femmes. Par ailleurs, cet événement accorde une place particulière à l’action sociale et solidaire, à travers l’organisation d’une campagne de circoncision au profit des enfants à l’hôpital provincial, accompagnée de la distribution de paniers d’aide aux familles des bénéficiaires. The post Le Moussem religieux et culturel de Moulay Abdellah Chérif, du 18 au 21 novembre à Ouezzane appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Fiscal surplus shrinks 40pc as revenues decline
items.description: • Primary surplus drops to 2.1pc of GDP from 2.8pc last year • Revenue falls despite higher tax collections; interest payments jump 23pc • Provincial cash surpluses shrink 23pc; Balochistan posts deficit ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s fiscal buffers weakened in the first quarter of the current fiscal year despite expenditure controls and subsidy cuts, as revenue-to-GDP ratios declined and provincial cash surpluses shrank. The overall fiscal surplus fell to 0.9 per cent of GDP in July-September this year from 1.7pc a year ago, according to fiscal operations data released by the Ministry of Finance. In absolute terms, the surplus declined by 40pc to Rs1.273 trillion in the first three months of the current fiscal year compared to Rs2.12tr a year earlier. The primary surplus — the difference between total revenue and expenditure excluding interest payments — also narrowed to 2.1pc of GDP from 2.8pc in the corresponding period last year. It stood at Rs2.97tr, down 15pc from Rs3.5tr in the first quarter of the previous fiscal year. Total revenue declined to 4.2pc of GDP from 4.9pc a year earlier. In a rare happening, revenue also fell in absolute terms to Rs6.004tr from Rs6.2tr, despite inflationary pressures and nominal economic growth that normally contribute to higher collections. The deterioration was reflected in both tax and non-tax revenue ratios, although the larger decline came from non-tax revenue, which fell to 1.8pc of GDP (Rs2.6tr) by the end of September 2026 compared to 2.4pc (Rs3.046tr) a year earlier. This was mainly due to lower State Bank profits, which dropped to Rs1.933tr from Rs2.43tr. However, petroleum receipts increased slightly to Rs382bn from Rs372bn. Tax revenue slipped to 2.4pc of GDP from 2.5pc a year earlier, although collections increased in absolute terms to Rs3.387tr from Rs3.153tr. On the expenditure side, total spending increased both as a percentage of GDP and in absolute terms. The expenditure-to-GDP ratio rose to 3.3pc from 3.2pc, while total expenditure increased by 16pc to Rs4.73tr from Rs4.08tr last year. Current expenditure declined as a share of GDP to 3pc from 3.2pc, although it increased in absolute terms to Rs4.293tr from Rs4.047tr. A major contributor to higher spending was the increase in interest payments, which rose by more than 23pc to Rs1.7tr from Rs1.378tr. As a share of GDP, these payments increased to 1.2pc from 1.1pc. Defence expenditure declined as a share of GDP to 0.3pc from 0.4pc, although it rose in absolute terms to Rs496bn from Rs447bn. Development expenditure remained unchanged at 0.3pc of GDP but increased to Rs468bn from Rs440bn. The data showed that subsidies were curtailed to Rs84.6bn (0.2pc of GDP) compared to Rs120bn (0.3pc) in the same period last year. Pension expenditure and the cost of running the civil government increased by 10pc and 6pc to Rs495bn and Rs263bn, respectively. Meanwhile, cash surpluses generated by the four provincial governments declined by 23pc to Rs600bn from Rs781bn last year. Punjab’s surplus fell to Rs333bn from Rs442bn, while Sindh’s surplus declined to Rs181bn from Rs209bn. However, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa increased its surplus by 33pc to Rs102bn from Rs77bn. Balochistan recorded a Rs16bn deficit in the first quarter against a surplus of Rs53bn in the corresponding period last year. The Ministry of Finance also reported a statistical discrepancy of Rs60bn in provincial accounts and attributed it to uncleared or delayed payments, late presentation of cheques relating to assignment accounts and movements in commercial bank deposits. A federal statistical discrepancy of Rs98bn was attributed to reporting time lags, book adjustments involving the State Bank of Pakistan, Federal Board of Reve­nue and Economic Affairs Division and a decline in commercial bank deposits. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: Sindh decides to replace petrol vehicles with EVs
items.description: KARACHI: The Sindh government has decided to gradually replace conventional vehicles used in government departments with electric vehicles (EVs), in a move aimed at cutting expenditure, saving fuel and reducing pollution. The decision was taken at a meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Austerity, chaired by Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon and attended by Local Government Minister Syed Nasir Hussain Shah. The meeting reviewed measures to reduce government expenditure, save fuel and assess the vehicle requirements of various departments. According to a press statement, the meeting decided to purchase vehicles for the home department, the Anti-Corruption Establishment and the universities and boards department, and agreed that electric vehicles would be given preference in future purchases for government departments. Mr Memon, who also holds the portfolios of information, transport and mass transit, said that saving official resources was among the provincial government’s priorities. He said that the provincial government wanted EVs to be given preference over conventional vehicles in future purchases and to gradually shift the entire government vehicle system to environment-friendly technology. “The future belongs to EVs and the Sindh government wants its institutions to adopt environment-friendly technology and reduce dependence on conventional fuels,” he added. The senior minister said that the gradual transition to EVs would also help reduce the day-to-day expenditure of government departments. The LG minister said that smoke emitted by conventional vehicles affected the urban environment and air quality. “We also want to promote the use of EVs instead of conventional vehicles in local government institutions,” he added. Published in Dawn, November 14th, 2026

items.title: AU Commission chairperson pays courtesy call on President Mahama
items.description: A high-level African Union (AU) Commission delegation led by Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf paid a courtesy call on President John Dramani Mahama, the incoming AU Chairperson, in Accra today. Mr Youssouf welcomed the opportunity to discuss key continental issues with the President. The delegation pledged full support to President Mahama as he assumes the AU Chairmanship in January. They recognised his leadership and significant contributions, especially his advocacy for reparative justice and commitment to reforming Africa’s financial institutions. The delegation expressed strong confidence that President Mahama’s leadership would make a substantial positive impact on the AU and shape its future direction constructively. A key topic was achieving financial self-reliance for the African Union. Citing ECOWAS as a successful model with a 0.5% levy to cover costs, President Mahama urged AU member states to fully implement the Union’s 0.2% levy on eligible imports. “It’s not government money to the AU; it’s the people’s money. Government is only a collecting agency,” President Mahama stated. They thanked President Mahama for supporting the AU’s efforts to achieve financial independence, especially through the proposed 0.2% levy on eligible imports to fund the Union’s work. President Mahama pledged to engage other African leaders to secure their full support for the levy’s implementation. He briefed the delegation on the Accra Reset Initiative, which seeks to advance Africa’s sovereignty and resilience by enhancing vaccine production, increasing access, and strengthening health systems across the continent. He reiterated the need to address Africa’s debt portfolio by exploring effective debt treatment approaches and creating sustainable mechanisms to manage the continent’s debt burden. The two leaders also discussed regional security and intra-African relations. Chairperson Youssouf commended President Mahama for his ongoing efforts to bridge divides between ECOWAS and the Alliance of Sahel States (AES). He also praised President Mahama’s leadership in advancing the AU’s reparations agenda worldwide.
